name: Bonaire
why: One of the world's best shore-diving destinations — dive right off the road at more than 60 marked sites, no boat needed. Marine park status since 1979 has kept reefs exceptionally healthy. Best: Year-round, outside the hurricane belt. Nicknamed "Diver's Paradise" — literally on the license plates — a genuine pilgrimage site for serious divers specifically for ease and reef health. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the birding list (Caribbean Flamingo) — a different animal.

name: Curaçao
why: The least-visited, arguably best-preserved of the ABC islands for diving — healthy reefs, easy shore access, and consistently calm water. Best: Year-round. Often rated above neighboring Aruba by serious divers, though less famous to general tourists. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Same region as the catalog's existing Aruba entry — a different, better-regarded-by-divers island.

name: Cayman Islands
why: Stingray City — dozens of wild southern stingrays in chest-deep water — is one of the most famous in-water wildlife encounters in the Caribbean. Bloody Bay Wall, off Little Cayman, is a legitimate world-class wall dive. Best: Year-round, driest Dec–Apr. A genuine dual identity — easy, family-friendly shallow water alongside serious wall diving. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the beaches list (Seven Mile Beach) — a different, non-diving claim on the same island.

name: Roatán & the Bay Islands
why: Part of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second-largest in the world — genuinely excellent, healthy reef diving at a fraction of the cost of the Caribbean's pricier destinations. Best: Year-round, calmest Mar–Sep. A long-standing reputation as one of the best value dive destinations on Earth. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Cozumel
why: Legendary drift-wall diving — Palancar and Santa Rosa walls are consistently named among the best in the world, with strong current doing the swimming for you. Best: Year-round, best visibility Apr–Sep. A globally recognized dive-specific destination, a short ferry from the mainland. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Same country as the catalog's existing Riviera Maya and Los Cabos entries — a genuinely distinct island, famous for a different kind of diving.

name: Dominica
why: Volcanic diving to match the island's landscape — hot springs bubble up through the seafloor at Champagne Reef, a genuinely unusual dive. Best: Year-round. Already famous for whale watching; the diving is a distinct, real reason to extend a stay. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the whale-watching list (same name; resident sperm whales), a different activity on the same island.

name: St. Vincent & the Grenadines
why: Sometimes called the muck-diving capital of the Caribbean — black volcanic sand hosting genuinely unusual small critters (frogfish, seahorses) that reef-focused destinations don't have. Best: Driest Dec–May. A real, specialist reputation among macro photographers, distinct from the postcard-reef image most of the Caribbean sells. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Socorro (Revillagigedo Islands)
why: Sometimes called "Mexico's Galápagos" — giant oceanic manta rays with wingspans over 20 feet approach divers directly, plus real chances at dolphins, sharks, and humpback whales. Best: Nov–May, peak Dec–Apr. Liveaboard-only, a specific pilgrimage for big-animal photographers, distinct from the Baja/Los Cabos coastal circuit already in the catalog. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Isla Guadalupe
why: The most reliable place on Earth for great white shark cage diving, thanks to exceptionally clear water. Best: Aug–Nov. A specific, single-species pilgrimage site. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the wildlife-viewing list.

name: Cocos Island
why: Massive schooling hammerhead sharks are the reason divers make the ~36-hour boat journey here — a genuinely remote, liveaboard-only national park. Best: Jun–Nov. One of the most famous big-animal liveaboard destinations in the Pacific, distinct from mainland Costa Rica's casual coastal diving already in the catalog. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the wildlife-viewing list.

name: Fernando de Noronha
why: Brazil's best diving and snorkeling by a wide margin — a resident spinner dolphin pod (the world's largest known, 1,000+ animals), turtles, and exceptionally clear water. Best: Driest and clearest Aug–Nov. A UNESCO World Heritage archipelago with visitor numbers capped by an environmental fee — genuinely distinct from Rio's modest coastal diving already in the catalog. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Same country as the catalog's existing Rio entry — a different region entirely.

name: Mozambique: Tofo and Bazaruto
why: A real, growing whale shark and manta ray destination — Tofo Beach is one of the most consistent places on Earth to swim with whale sharks. Best: Whale sharks year-round, best Oct–Mar; mantas year-round. A genuine, still-developing alternative to the pricier Maldives/Seychelles for the same animals. (Emerging. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Sodwana Bay & Aliwal Shoal
why: Warm Indian Ocean reef diving on South Africa's opposite coast from Cape Town. Sodwana Bay is the northern reef base; ragged-tooth sharks gather at Aliwal Shoal, near Durban, a separate base several hours south. Best: Sharks Jun–Nov; general diving year-round. A genuinely different coast, climate, and diving style — warm tropical reef, not cold kelp forest — from the country's existing catalog entries. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Same country as the catalog's existing Cape Town and Kruger entries — the opposite, warm-water coast.

name: Djibouti
why: Whale sharks gather here with unusual reliability, in a small country most travelers have never considered. Best: Oct–Feb. One of the most predictable whale shark aggregations on Earth, genuinely under-visited. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Mafia Island
why: A quieter, less-developed alternative to Zanzibar with a real, dedicated whale shark season. Best: Whale sharks Oct–Feb. A real marine park, genuinely distinct from the country's main tourist circuit. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Same country as the catalog's existing Tanzania entry — a different island, season, and animal from its Mnemba Atoll content.

name: Musandam Peninsula
why: Called the "Norway of Arabia" for its fjord-like coastline — genuinely good, still-uncrowded coral diving in the Strait of Hormuz. Best: Oct–Apr. A real, growing dive destination, distinct from the rest of the country. (Emerging. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Same country as the whale-watching list's Salalah & Dhofar and the wildlife-viewing list's Ras al Jinz — a different, northern region from both.

name: Layang-Layang
why: A remote standalone atoll resort — sheer walls dropping over 6,500 feet, and schooling scalloped hammerhead sharks that draw serious pelagic divers specifically for them. Best: Open Mar–Aug only; hammerheads peak Apr–May. Access is by charter flight and the resort itself only operates part of the year — a real, if narrow, pilgrimage site distinct from the catalog's existing Malaysian Borneo entry (Sipadan), a different sea entirely. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Andaman Islands
why: Havelock Island has genuinely good, healthy reef diving — a real, if still under-the-radar, alternative to Southeast Asia's more crowded dive hubs. Best: Nov–Apr. A distinct part of India from every existing catalog entry (Kerala, Rajasthan, Kaziranga, Ladakh), none of which are dive-focused. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Wakatobi
why: An exceptionally remote, private marine reserve with some of the healthiest reef in Indonesia — access is by chartered flight, and it's built entirely around diving. Best: Apr–Nov. Consistently rated by serious divers among the best reef health anywhere in the world, precisely because it's so hard to reach. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Lembeh Strait
why: The macro-diving capital of the world — black volcanic sand hosting an extraordinary concentration of small, bizarre critters (mimic octopus, hairy frogfish, flamboyant cuttlefish) that reef divers never see. Best: Year-round. A genuine pilgrimage for underwater macro photographers specifically, distinct from Indonesia's reef-scenery destinations already in the catalog (Bali, Komodo, Raja Ampat). (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Yap
why: Manta rays visit cleaning stations here reliably nearly year-round, in the channel right by the main town — no boat ride required. Best: Best visibility Dec–Apr; mantas present year-round. A genuine specialist pilgrimage for manta encounters, distinct from Palau's own manta site (German Channel) already in the catalog. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Chuuk (Truk) Lagoon
why: The largest, most intact collection of shipwrecks anywhere on Earth — an entire WWII Japanese fleet sunk in a single 1944 raid, sitting largely undisturbed in shallow, warm water. Best: Year-round, calmest Dec–Apr. Widely considered wreck diving's single most legendary destination. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Solomon Islands
why: Genuinely pristine reef alongside real WWII wreck diving — much of the fighting around Guadalcanal happened in these waters. Best: Apr–Nov. One of the least-touristed, highest-quality reef systems left in the Pacific. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Vanuatu
why: The SS President Coolidge, an American troopship sunk in 1942, is one of the most famous and most penetrable wreck dives in the world — divable largely by swimming in through actual ship doorways. Best: Apr–Oct. A genuine bucket-list wreck for advanced divers specifically. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Bikini Atoll
why: The wrecks of an entire fleet sunk by 1946 nuclear weapons tests, including a sunken aircraft carrier — among the most legendary wreck dives on Earth. Best: Apr–Oct. Extremely low-volume and expensive, reached only by a small number of technical divers, but genuinely mythic among serious wreck divers. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: New Caledonia
why: One of the largest lagoons on Earth (a UNESCO World Heritage site), with real, varied reef diving and a genuine dugong population. Best: Apr–Dec. A real, substantial dive destination in its own right, not just a scenic backdrop. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the birding list (the Kagu) — a different, non-marine animal, same country.

name: Cook Islands
why: Real, healthy reef diving plus a genuine humpback whale season, in a much less developed, less visited part of Polynesia than Bora Bora or Tahiti. Best: Whales Jul–Oct; reef diving year-round. A real, quieter alternative within the same ocean as the catalog's existing French Polynesia entry. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

name: Ningaloo Reef
why: One of the world's few places to swim with whale sharks reliably, plus a genuine, healthy fringing reef accessible directly from shore — no boat required for much of it. Best: Whale sharks Mar–Jul; reef diving year-round. A UNESCO-listed reef with a real, distinct identity from the Great Barrier Reef already in the catalog. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the whale-watching list (humpback whale migration) and the wildlife-viewing list (whale sharks, a different season) — three separate, real claims on the same reef.

name: Cape Verde Islands
why: Real but modest volcanic-island diving and some wrecks — genuinely not in the same tier as the Caribbean or Indo-Pacific, but a real, distinct Atlantic destination. Best: Year-round, calmest Feb–Jun. More often visited for its music and beaches, but the diving is real, if modest. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the birding list (Cape Verde Shearwater, Raso Lark).

name: Cebu & the Visayas
why: A huge shoal of sardines sits just off Moalboal beach and is near-guaranteed all year, and divers reach it from the shore. Malapascua, a short trip north, is known for thresher sharks that visit cleaning stations at Monad Shoal around sunrise; Moalboal itself rarely sees them. Best: Dec–May for weather, visibility and sardine action; water 80–86°F year-round. (Established. Added 11 Oct 2026, web-checked.)

name: Malta & Gozo
why: Year-round Mediterranean diving built around wrecks and caves: the Um El Faroud tanker (about 330 feet long, around 115 feet down), the Blue Hole and arch on Gozo, and the boulder field left where the Azure Window collapsed in 2017. Best: April–October, water about 57–82°F; winter diving continues but is windier. (Established. Added 11 Oct 2026, web-checked.)

name: Florida Keys
why: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, the first underwater park in the US, with the Christ of the Abyss statue in shallow water (snorkelers can see it), Molasses Reef, and the 510-foot USS Spiegel Grove wreck for advanced divers off Key Largo. Best: spring through fall; summer is warmest and calmest, fall brings coral spawning; visibility can swing quickly. (Established. Added 11 Oct 2026, web-checked.)

name: Gili Islands & Lombok
why: Green and hawksbill turtles are close to guaranteed on Gili Trawangan and Gili Meno, with an easy, mild-current reef that suits learners and a turtle sanctuary on Gili Meno. Reef sharks on the deeper drift dives; manta rays visit late in the year. Best: year-round, water 81–84°F. (Established. Added 11 Oct 2026, web-checked.)

name: British Virgin Islands
why: The RMS Rhone, a 310-foot Royal Mail steamship that sank in a hurricane in 1867, lies off Salt Island in a marine park, with the bow around 75 feet down and the stern at 30–60 feet. Anegada has a long, little-visited horseshoe reef and older wrecks. Best: December–April for the driest weather. (Established. Added 11 Oct 2026, web-checked.)

name: Anilao
why: One of the best-known muck and macro dive areas in the Philippines, about 2.5–3 hours south of Manila: seahorses, mimic and blue-ringed octopus, frogfish, nudibranchs, and mandarin fish on night dives; Secret Bay is the signature site. Best: November–December and April–May, the main season runs October to early June; water is cooler January–March, often with more critters. (Real, specialist-known. Added 11 Oct 2026, web-checked.)

name: Vava'u
why: One of the very few places where in-water swims with humpback whales are legally allowed; mothers and calves rest here after the migration from Antarctica. Best: July–October, peak September–October when the seas are calmest. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist, whale list.) ↳ Also on the whale-watching list (same name); here the draw is the in-water swim.
